chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Repertoire pressure at the Vanguard and her total four years
summary: She mixed standards with her hit songs and ran into audiences from different countries; she worked there off and on until 1956.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: So do you get pressures on you here to get back into the "Loch Lomond" mold. I was doing "If I Had A Ribbon Blow" and "Molly Malone" but

/ I was still doing quite a few standard pop tunes too. I had more time. I could do anything I wanted to. Those were, more or less, my highlights of the performance, these were the things that people came in and requested. You know, the Village Vanguard, there are people that come to New York that never get up to mid-town. They get off the boat somewhere down there in the Village and they make the Village scene. And I

ran into a lot of people from different countries that had heard my recordings. In fact they said that they sort of anticipated these recordings because they were sort of scarce and I believe they were just issuing a small number of my recordings at a time. We got a lot of people from out of the Country visiting the Vanguard, which was a good experience too.
Okay, so you mixed your repertoire?

Yes. You know me, I sing standard but I like to pick out the goodies, you know. But it was during the time that I was at the Vanguard, that last engagement, that a friend of mine said, you want to go and hear the new music and the new music was bop. It was during the time I was at the Vanguard when Dizzy opened at the Royal Roost on Broadway and they were introducing The Bop. I didn't dig it, you know.
What year was this, do you know?
I have no idea. But it was just when they were beginning to sell Bop. Of course the musicians, they had been around, but it was just a new style. And they had little brochures on the table

explaining what it was. And they were also selling chicken in the basket. The war was over and there were allot of ex-GI's and business was good. What really struck me, that night I was there they were playing Bop all over the place and I didn't dig it. It was kind of noisy too. But the trumpet player, I don't even know what his name was. I think his last name was Green, I don't know. But he did a solo. He did, 'Please Give Me Something To Remember You By' and a hush fell over the place. So that gave me some hopes, so after all sweet music hasn't gone anyplace, it's still around. So that was one of the experiences I had.
Okay. So you stayed four years?
Oh, until 1956, because in 1956, at the end of '56 I went out to Hawaii and came back in '57 and that's when I stopped singing.
Okay, not consecutively, a total of four years.
